use: Polite reply when someone explains something or asks you to do something; with friends, say wakatta.

example.romaji: hai, wakarimashita. ashita made ni yarimasu.
example.ja: はい、わかりました。明日までにやります。
example.english: Okay, understood. I'll have it done by tomorrow.

notes: To a boss or customer, shouchi shimashita or kashikomarimashita sounds more formal.

english: I don't understand; I don't know
use: Polite way to say you don't follow or can't answer; with friends, say wakannai.

example.romaji: sumimasen, nihongo ga yoku wakarimasen.
example.ja: すみません、日本語がよくわかりません。
example.english: Sorry, I don't really understand Japanese.

notes: For facts, shirimasen also means 'I don't know' but can sound cold; wakarimasen is softer.

use: A cheerful drawn-out yes, called back when someone calls your name or asks you to do something; shop staff use it too.

example.romaji: haai, ima iku kara chotto matte!
example.ja: はーい、今行くからちょっと待って！
example.english: Coming! Just a sec!

examplePolite.ja: はーい、今すぐ行きます！

notes: A short hai is the plain yes; haai sounds friendly, or childish if overused.

use: Quick okay to a plan or instruction, very common in texts between friends and coworkers.

example.romaji: ryoukai, ja eki de matteru ne.
example.ja: 了解、じゃ駅で待ってるね。
example.english: Got it, I'll wait at the station then.

examplePolite.romaji: ryoukai shimashita. eki de matte imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 了解しました。駅で待っています。
examplePolite.english: Understood. I'll wait at the station.

notes: Some people find ryoukai shimashita too blunt for a boss; shouchi shimashita is safer upward.

src: もう一度お願いします
ja: もう一度お願いします
kana: もういちどおねがいします
english: once more, please; could you say that again?
use: Ask someone to repeat what they said; staff and teachers hear it from learners all the time.

example.romaji: sumimasen, mou ichido onegai shimasu.
example.ja: すみません、もう一度お願いします。
example.english: Sorry, could you say that again?

notes: Casual: mou ikkai itte. Add yukkuri (slowly) if speed is the problem.

english: I didn't catch that; I couldn't hear
use: When noise or a quiet voice is the problem; usually followed by a request to repeat.

example.romaji: gomen, kikoenakatta. mou ikkai itte?
example.ja: ごめん、聞こえなかった。もう一回言って？
example.english: Sorry, I didn't catch that. Say it again?

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kikoemasen deshita. mou ichido onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、聞こえませんでした。もう一度お願いします。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I couldn't hear. Once more, please.

notes: kikoeru is 'can be heard'; kiku is 'listen' or 'ask'.

src: ゆっくり話してください
ja: ゆっくり話してください
kana: ゆっくりはなしてください
use: Ask a fast speaker to slow down; mou sukoshi (a bit more) makes it softer.

example.romaji: sumimasen, mou sukoshi yukkuri hanashite kudasai.
example.ja: すみません、もう少しゆっくり話してください。
example.english: Sorry, could you speak a little more slowly?

notes: With friends, just yukkuri itte.

kana: にほんごじょうずですね
use: Said to learners, often after only a few words; answer iie, mada mada desu (no, I've a long way to go).

example.romaji: e, nihongo jouzu desu ne! doko de benkyou shita n desu ka?
example.ja: え、日本語上手ですね！どこで勉強したんですか？
example.english: Oh, your Japanese is good! Where did you learn?

notes: Usually politeness, not a real assessment. Friends say nihongo umai ne.

use: Eager agreement when someone says what you were thinking; also opens something you just remembered.

example.romaji: sou sou, sore ga iitakatta no!
example.ja: そうそう、それが言いたかったの！
example.english: Yes, exactly, that's what I was trying to say!

examplePolite.romaji: sou sou, sore ga iitakatta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: そうそう、それが言いたかったんです。
examplePolite.english: Yes, exactly, that's what I was trying to say.

notes: A single sou desu ne is calmer agreement.

use: Confirms someone has guessed or summed it up correctly, often from the person who made the point.

example.romaji: sono toori, sore ga ichiban daiji na n da yo.
example.ja: その通り、それが一番大事なんだよ。
example.english: Exactly, that's what matters most.

examplePolite.romaji: sono toori desu. sore ga ichiban daiji na n desu.
examplePolite.ja: その通りです。それが一番大事なんです。
examplePolite.english: That's right. That's what matters most.

notes: To a boss or customer: ossharu toori desu.

english: I know, I know; I totally get it
use: Sympathy when a friend describes a feeling or situation you've had too.

example.romaji: wakaru wakaru, getsuyoubi tte honto ni darui yo ne.
example.ja: わかるわかる、月曜日ってほんとにだるいよね。
example.english: I know, right? Mondays are such a drag.

notes: It means 'I feel the same', not 'I understand your words'.

ja: おっしゃるとおりです
kana: おっしゃるとおりです
english: you're quite right; exactly as you say
use: Respectful agreement to a boss, client or customer, often before an apology or a fix.

example.romaji: ossharu toori desu. sugu ni naoshimasu.
example.ja: おっしゃるとおりです。すぐに直します。
example.english: You're quite right. I'll fix it right away.

notes: ossharu is the respectful form of iu (say). Among friends, sono toori is enough.

use: Past tense because it describes how you feel now; often a sigh at the end of the day.

example.romaji: aa, tsukareta. kyou wa hayaku neyou.
example.ja: ああ、疲れた。今日は早く寝よう。
example.english: Ugh, I'm tired. I'm going to bed early tonight.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa chotto tsukaremashita. hayaku nemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はちょっと疲れました。早く寝ます。
examplePolite.english: I'm a bit tired today. I'll go to bed early.

notes: Related: otsukare, the 'good work' greeting at the end of a job or day.

kana: ぜんぜんだいじょうぶ
english: totally fine; no problem at all
use: Reassure someone who apologizes or asks if you're okay.

example.romaji: un, zenzen daijoubu da yo. ki ni shinaide.
example.ja: うん、全然大丈夫だよ。気にしないで。
example.english: Yeah, totally fine. Don't worry about it.

examplePolite.romaji: hai, zenzen daijoubu desu. ki ni shinaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: はい、全然大丈夫です。気にしないでください。
examplePolite.english: Yes, totally fine. Please don't worry about it.

notes: Textbooks say zenzen needs a negative, but zenzen daijoubu is normal everyday speech.

use: Said on waking with a stretch, or as the answer to yoku neta? (did you sleep well?).

example.romaji: un, yuube wa yoku neta yo. arigatou.
example.ja: うん、ゆうべはよく寝たよ。ありがとう。
example.english: Yeah, I slept well last night, thanks.

examplePolite.romaji: hai, okagesama de yuube wa yoku nemashita.
examplePolite.ja: はい、おかげさまでゆうべはよく寝ました。
examplePolite.english: Yes, thanks, I slept well last night.

notes: Politely, people also ask and answer with yoku nemuremashita (were able to sleep well).

use: Explains why you're tired or out of it today.

example.romaji: kinou zenzen nemurenakatta. ima sugoku nemui.
example.ja: 昨日全然眠れなかった。今すごく眠い。
example.english: I couldn't sleep at all last night. I'm so sleepy now.

examplePolite.ja: 昨日はあまり眠れませんでした。
examplePolite.english: I didn't sleep very well last night.

notes: nerarenakatta means the same and is just as common.

use: Blunt everyday way to say you're hungry, mostly among male friends and family.

example.romaji: aa, hara hetta. nanka tabe ni ikou.
example.ja: ああ、腹減った。なんか食べに行こう。
example.english: Man, I'm starving. Let's go grab something.

notes: Neutral: onaka suita. Polite: onaka ga sukimashita.

use: Say when you can't eat any more, or to turn down seconds.

example.romaji: mou onaka ippai, taberarenai.
example.ja: もうお腹いっぱい、食べられない。
example.english: I'm full, I can't eat another bite.

examplePolite.romaji: mou onaka ippai desu. gochisousama deshita.
examplePolite.ja: もうお腹いっぱいです。ごちそうさまでした。
examplePolite.english: I'm full. Thank you for the meal.

notes: Also figurative: 'I've had enough of that'.

use: Literally 'my throat has dried'; the everyday way to say you want a drink.

example.romaji: nodo kawaita, nanka nomou yo.
example.ja: 喉渇いた、なんか飲もうよ。
example.english: I'm thirsty, let's get a drink.

examplePolite.romaji: nodo ga kawakimashita ne. nanika nomimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 喉が渇きましたね。何か飲みませんか？
examplePolite.english: I'm thirsty. Shall we get something to drink?

notes: Past tense because it describes the state now, like tsukareta.

use: Soft, cute way to say you're very hungry; fine for anyone, common with kids.

example.romaji: mou onaka pekopeko, hayaku tabeyou!
example.ja: もうお腹ペコペコ、早く食べよう！
example.english: I'm starving, let's eat already!

examplePolite.romaji: mou onaka pekopeko desu. hayaku tabemashou.
examplePolite.ja: もうお腹ペコペコです。早く食べましょう。

notes: Gentler than hara hetta; pekopeko is the sound-word for an empty stomach.
